title: Τεῦκρος καὶ Αἴας
titleEn: The Fight at the Sterns and Teucer’s Bow — Iliad 15.377–470
part: The Fight at the Sterns and Teucer’s Bow (15.377–470)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Zeus thunders in answer to Nestor’s prayer, and the Trojans, hearing it, pour down over the wall like a wave over a ship’s side and fight at the sterns of the ships. In Eurypylus’ hut Patroclus sees the rush and leaves the wounded man, resolving to go and try to rouse Achilles. At the ships the fighting stays level, and Hector and Ajax struggle over a single ship. Ajax kills Caletor as he brings fire, and Hector, calling the Trojans to save the body, throws at Ajax and misses, killing instead Lycophron, Ajax’s attendant. Ajax calls Teucer, who comes with his bow and shoots Cleitus from his chariot; Polydamas takes the team in hand. Teucer then takes aim at Hector, but Zeus guards Hector and breaks the bowstring, and Teucer cries out that some power is cutting short their plans.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, μέγα δ’ ἔκτυπε μητίετα Ζεύς,
ἀράων ἀΐων Νηληϊάδαο γέροντος.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’ euchomenos, mega d’ ektype mētieta Zeus,
araōn aïōn Nēlēïadao gerontos.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, praying, and greatly thundered counsellor Zeus,
hearing the prayers of the old man, Neleus’-son.
sentences.i: So he spoke in prayer, and Zeus the counsellor thundered loudly, hearing the prayers of the old man, the son of Neleus.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος ‘so he spoke, praying’ is the formula that closes Nestor’s prayer, and Zeus answers with thunder: μέγα is adverbial ‘loudly’, and ἔκτυπε is the aorist of κτυπέω ‘thunder’ (the root of κτύπον in the next line). μητίετα is the epic nominative of the stock ‘counsellor’. ἀράων is the genitive plural of ἀρά ‘prayer’, the object of ἀΐων ‘hearing’, and Νηληϊάδαο γέροντος ‘the old man, Neleus’ son’ is Nestor, the patronymic in epic -αο.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’ ὡς ἐπύθοντο Διὸς κτύπον αἰγιόχοιο,
μᾶλλον ἐπ’ Ἀργείοισι θόρον, μνήσαντο δὲ χάρμης.
sentences.tr:
Trōes d’ hōs epythonto Dios ktypon aigiochoio,
mallon ep’ Argeioisi thoron, mnēsanto de charmēs.
sentences.l:
And the Trojans, when they heard the thunder of aegis-bearing Zeus,
the more upon the Argives leapt, and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.i: And when the Trojans heard the thunder of aegis-bearing Zeus, they leapt the more upon the Argives and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.n: Διὸς κτύπον αἰγιόχοιο ‘the thunder of aegis-bearing Zeus’ is the object of ἐπύθοντο, the aorist of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn’, here learn by hearing. μᾶλλον ‘the more’ is the comparative of μάλα; θόρον is an unaugmented aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’ (Attic ἔθορον), and Ἀργείοισι is the epic dative plural in -οισι. μνήσαντο δὲ χάρμης ‘and remembered the joy of battle’ is the aorist middle of μιμνῄσκομαι with the genitive. For the Trojans the thunder is a sign that Zeus is on their side.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὥς τε μέγα κῦμα θαλάσσης εὐρυπόροιο
νηὸς ὑπὲρ τοίχων καταβήσεται, ὁππότ’ ἐπείγῃ
ἲς ἀνέμου· ἣ γάρ τε μάλιστά γε κύματ’ ὀφέλλει·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hōs te mega kyma thalassēs euryporoio
nēos hyper toichōn katabēsetai, hoppot’ epeigēi
is anemou· hē gar te malista ge kymat’ ophellei·
sentences.i: As a great wave of the wide-wayed sea comes down over the sides of a ship when the force of the wind drives it on—for that force, above all, makes the waves grow—
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ means the Trojans, but the sentence turns at once into a simile, and the Trojans do not return until ὣς Τρῶες in line 384. The picture is a great wave coming down over a ship’s side (τοίχων, the sides of the ship) when the wind presses hard: ὁππότ’ ἐπείγῃ is a subjunctive, and καταβήσεται is a future form, used for what a wave does whenever the wind is behind it. ἲς ἀνέμου ‘the force of the wind’ is a periphrasis for the wind itself, and ἣ ‘that’ points back to it. ὀφέλλει ‘increases’ gives the reason: of all things it is the wind that most makes waves grow. εὐρυπόροιο ‘wide-wayed’ is εὐρύς ‘wide’ with πόρος ‘passage’.

sentences.t: ὣς Τρῶες μεγάλῃ ἰαχῇ κατὰ τεῖχος ἔβαινον,
sentences.tr: hōs Trōes megalēi iachēi kata teichos ebainon,
sentences.l: so the Trojans with a great cry down over the wall went,
sentences.i: so the Trojans, with a great cry, kept coming down over the wall,
sentences.n: ὣς Τρῶες ‘so the Trojans’ closes the simile: they pour down over the wall as the wave comes down over the ship’s side. μεγάλῃ ἰαχῇ is the dative of ἰαχή ‘cry’, here the battle-cry. κατὰ τεῖχος with the accusative is ‘down over the wall’, and ἔβαινον is the imperfect of βαίνω, so ‘kept coming’.

sentences.t:
ἵππους δ’ εἰσελάσαντες ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσι μάχοντο
ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοις αὐτοσχεδόν, οἳ μὲν ἀφ’ ἵππων,
sentences.tr:
hippous d’ eiselasantes epi prymnēisi machonto
enchesin amphigyois autoschedon, hoi men aph’ hippōn,
sentences.l:
and having driven the horses in, at the sterns they fought
with double-pointed spears at close quarters, some from horses,
sentences.i: and driving their horses in, they fought at the ships’ sterns at close quarters with double-pointed spears, some from their horses,
sentences.n: ἵππους … εἰσελάσαντες is ‘having driven the horses in’ (εἰσελαύνω), so the Trojans fight right at the ships’ sterns (ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσι, the plural of πρύμνη ‘stern’). ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοις ‘with double-pointed spears’: ἀμφίγυος is a word of unknown meaning, and ‘pointed at both ends’ is the usual guess. αὐτοσχεδόν ‘at close quarters’ is the adverb of hand-to-hand fighting. οἳ μὲν ἀφ’ ἵππων ‘some from horses’ opens a pair that the next unit completes with οἳ δ’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀπὸ νηῶν ὕψι μελαινάων ἐπιβάντες
μακροῖσι ξυστοῖσι, τά ῥά σφ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἔκειτο
ναύμαχα κολλήεντα, κατὰ στόμα εἱμένα χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ apo nēōn hypsi melainaōn epibantes
makroisi xystoisi, ta rha sph’ epi nēusin ekeito
naumacha kollēenta, kata stoma heimena chalkōi.
sentences.l:
others from black ships, high up, having mounted,
with long polished spears, which for them on the ships lay,
ship-fighting, glued, at the point clothed in bronze.
sentences.i: while others, standing high up on the black ships, fought with long polished spears that lay for them on the ships, made for fighting at sea, glued together and clothed in bronze at the tip.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘others’ answers οἳ μὲν in the last unit. ἐπιβάντες is the aorist participle of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step up on’, and ὕψι ‘high up’ places these men on the ships. The weapons are ξυστά ‘polished spears’, μακρά ‘long’: τά ῥά σφ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶν ἔκειτο is ‘which lay for them (σφι, elided) on the ships’. ναύμαχα is ‘ship-fighting’, κολλήεντα ‘glued’ (κόλλα ‘glue’; the Greek does not say what was glued), and κατὰ στόμα εἱμένα χαλκῷ ‘clothed in bronze at the point’ (στόμα ‘mouth’, here the tip; εἱμένα is the perfect passive participle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’).

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ εἷος μὲν Ἀχαιοί τε Τρῶές τε
τείχεος ἀμφεμάχοντο θοάων ἔκτοθι νηῶν,
sentences.tr:
Patroklos d’ heios men Achaioi te Trōes te
teicheos amphemachonto thoaōn ektothi nēōn,
sentences.l:
Now Patroclus, so long as the Achaeans and the Trojans
about the wall were fighting, outside the swift ships,
sentences.i: Now Patroclus, for as long as the Achaeans and the Trojans were fighting around the wall, outside the swift ships,
sentences.n: The scene changes to Patroclus, who is in the hut of the wounded Eurypylus (named in the next unit). εἷος is the epic form of ἕως ‘as long as’; it is answered by τόφρα ‘for so long’ at the start of the next unit. ἀμφεμάχοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀμφιμάχομαι ‘fight around’, with τείχεος (epic genitive -εος) ‘around the wall’, and ἔκτοθι θοάων … νηῶν is ‘outside the swift ships’.

sentences.t:
τόφρ’ ὅ γ’ ἐνὶ κλισίῃ ἀγαπήνορος Εὐρυπύλοιο
ἧστό τε καὶ τὸν ἔτερπε λόγοις, ἐπὶ δ’ ἕλκεϊ λυγρῷ
φάρμακ’ ἀκέσματ’ ἔπασσε μελαινάων ὀδυνάων.
sentences.tr:
tophr’ ho g’ eni klisiēi agapēnoros Eurypyloio
hēsto te kai ton eterpe logois, epi d’ helkeï lygrōi
pharmak’ akesmat’ epasse melainaōn odynaōn.
sentences.l:
for so long he in the hut of man-cherishing Eurypylus
sat, and delighted him with talk, and on the grievous wound
drugs, remedies of the black pains, was sprinkling.
sentences.i: for that long he sat in the hut of Eurypylus, who prized manliness, and cheered him with talk, and sprinkled on his grievous wound the drugs that are remedies for the black pains.
sentences.n: τόφρ’ ‘for so long’ answers εἷος, and ὅ γ’ is Patroclus. ἀγαπήνορος is the stock epithet of Eurypylus, ‘man-cherishing’, and its sense is not known (‘prizing manliness’ is a guess). ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’; τὸν ἔτερπε λόγοις is ‘delighted him with talk’ (τέρπω ‘delight’), so Patroclus is keeping the wounded man cheerful. ἐπὶ δ’ … ἔπασσε is ‘sprinkled on’, split in two (ἐπιπάσσω), with ἕλκεϊ λυγρῷ ‘the grievous wound’ (dative of ἕλκος). φάρμακ’ ἀκέσματα ‘drugs, remedies’ (ἀκέσματα from ἀκέομαι ‘heal’), and μελαινάων ὀδυνάων ‘of the black pains’ depends on ἀκέσματα.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τεῖχος ἐπεσσυμένους ἐνόησε
Τρῶας, ἀτὰρ Δαναῶν γένετο ἰαχή τε φόβος τε,
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē teichos epessymenous enoēse
Trōas, atar Danaōn geneto iachē te phobos te,
sentences.l:
but when he perceived the Trojans rushing
on the wall, and of the Danaans came a cry and terror,
sentences.i: but when he saw the Trojans rushing at the wall, and a cry and terror rose among the Danaans,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ … ἐνόησε is ‘but when he perceived’, with Patroclus as the subject (the singular verb), and the main verb comes in the next unit. Τρῶας is the object, ἐπεσσυμένους ‘rushing on’ is a participle of ἐπισεύομαι, and τεῖχος is the accusative of direction, ‘at the wall’. Δαναῶν γένετο ἰαχή τε φόβος τε is ‘of the Danaans there arose a cry and terror’; the genitive says among whom. The same line stands in an earlier part, with a plural verb.

sentences.t:
ᾤμωξέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα καὶ ὣ πεπλήγετο μηρὼ
χερσὶ καταπρηνέσσ’, ὀλοφυρόμενος δ’ ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
ōimōxen t’ ar’ epeita kai hō peplēgeto mērō
chersi kataprēness’, olophyromenos d’ epos ēuda·
sentences.l:
and cried out then, and struck his own two thighs
with downturned hands, and lamenting a word he spoke:
sentences.i: He cried out, and struck both his thighs with the flats of his hands, and as he lamented he spoke:
sentences.n: ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘cry out in grief’, and πεπλήγετο is a Homeric past of πλήσσω ‘strike’, middle because he strikes his own body. ὣ is the dual possessive ‘his own two’, agreeing with μηρώ ‘thighs’ (dual). χερσὶ καταπρηνέσσ’ is ‘with downturned hands’ (καταπρηνής, the epic dative plural -εσσι); striking the thighs with the flat of the hand is the gesture of grief. ὀλοφυρόμενος is ‘lamenting’, and ἔπος ηὔδα ‘spoke a word’ is the stock opening of a speech. Its second line is word for word the second line of Ares’ gesture at 15.113.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύπυλ’ οὐκ ἔτι τοι δύναμαι χατέοντί περ’ ἔμπης
ἐνθάδε παρμενέμεν· δὴ γὰρ μέγα νεῖκος ὄρωρεν·
sentences.tr:
Eurypyl’ ouk eti toi dynamai chateonti per’ empēs
enthade parmenemen· dē gar mega neikos orōren·
sentences.l:
“Eurypylus, no longer for you am I able, though you are in need, all the same,
here to stay beside you; for now a great quarrel has arisen;
sentences.i: “Eurypylus, I can no longer stay here beside you, though you are in need, all the same; for a great quarrel has now arisen;
sentences.n: Patroclus’ speech to Eurypylus begins. Εὐρύπυλ’ is the vocative. οὐκ ἔτι τοι δύναμαι … παρμενέμεν is ‘I can no longer stay beside you’ (παρμενέμεν is παραμένειν with the epic infinitive ending -μεν; τοι is σοι). χατέοντί περ is ‘though you are in need’ (χατέω ‘need’, dative participle agreeing with τοι), and ἔμπης is ‘all the same’. δὴ γὰρ μέγα νεῖκος ὄρωρεν is ‘for now a great quarrel has arisen’: νεῖκος is ‘quarrel’, here the fighting itself, and ὄρωρεν is the perfect of ὄρνυμι.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὲ μὲν θεράπων ποτιτερπέτω, αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε
σπεύσομαι εἰς Ἀχιλῆα, ἵν’ ὀτρύνω πολεμίζειν.
sentences.tr:
alla se men therapōn potiterpetō, autar egōge
speusomai eis Achilēa, hin’ otrynō polemizein.
sentences.l:
but you, let an attendant go on delighting, while I myself
will hasten to Achilles, that I may urge him to fight.
sentences.i: but let an attendant go on cheering you, while I myself hurry to Achilles to urge him to fight.
sentences.n: ἀλλά … μέν … αὐτάρ sets ‘you’ against ‘I myself’. θεράπων is an ‘attendant’, and ποτιτερπέτω is the third-person imperative of ποτιτέρπω (ποτί is the epic form of πρός, ‘besides’), ‘let him go on delighting’. σπεύσομαι is the future of σπεύδω ‘hasten’, and Ἀχιλῆα has a single λ for the metre. ἵν’ ὀτρύνω is a purpose clause with the short-vowel subjunctive of ὀτρύνω ‘urge’, and πολεμίζειν is ‘to fight’.

sentences.t:
τίς δ’ οἶδ’ εἴ κέν οἱ σὺν δαίμονι θυμὸν ὀρίνω
παρειπών;
sentences.tr:
tis d’ oid’ ei ken hoi syn daimoni thymon orinō
pareipōn;
sentences.l:
And who knows whether, with some power, his heart I may stir,
talking him round?
sentences.i: And who knows whether, with some power’s help, I may stir his heart by talking him round?
sentences.n: τίς δ’ οἶδ’ εἴ κέν … ὀρίνω is ‘who knows whether perhaps I may stir’: εἰ κεν with the short-vowel subjunctive of ὀρίνω ‘stir’, and θυμόν is his heart. σὺν δαίμονι ‘with some power’s help’: δαίμων is an unnamed divine power helping a man. παρειπών is the aorist participle of παραείπον ‘talk round, persuade’. The mark printed as a semicolon is the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: ἀγαθὴ δὲ παραίφασίς ἐστιν ἑταίρου.
sentences.tr: agathē de paraiphasis estin hetairou.
sentences.l: good is the persuasion of a companion.
sentences.i: a companion’s persuasion is a good thing.
sentences.n: The speech closes on a saying. παραίφασις is ‘persuasion’ (a rare noun from παραφημί ‘talk round, encourage’, so ‘talking round’, which echoes παρειπών just before), ἀγαθή is ‘good’, and ἑταίρου ‘of a companion’ is the genitive, so: a friend’s persuasion is good. Patroclus is Achilles’ companion, and that is what he hopes to use.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰπόντα πόδες φέρον·
sentences.tr: ton men ar’ hōs eiponta podes pheron·
sentences.l: Him then, so having spoken, his feet bore;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his feet bore him away;
sentences.n: τὸν … εἰπόντα is ‘him, having so spoken’, the object of φέρον, whose subject is πόδες ‘feet’. πόδες φέρον ‘his feet bore him’ is a stock way of saying that someone set off, and φέρον is the unaugmented imperfect of φέρω. μὲν … αὐτάρ sets Patroclus against the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
Τρῶας ἐπερχομένους μένον ἔμπεδον, οὐδ’ ἐδύναντο
παυροτέρους περ ἐόντας ἀπώσασθαι παρὰ νηῶν·
sentences.tr:
autar Achaioi
Trōas eperchomenous menon empedon, oud’ edynanto
pauroterous per eontas apōsasthai para nēōn·
sentences.i: but the Achaeans awaited the Trojans steadily as they came on, and were unable to push them back from the ships, fewer though the Trojans were;
sentences.n: μένον is the unaugmented imperfect of μένω, here with the accusative ‘awaited’: Τρῶας ἐπερχομένους ‘the Trojans coming on’ (ἐπέρχομαι), ἔμπεδον ‘steadily’. οὐδ’ ἐδύναντο is ‘nor were they able’, and the infinitive is ἀπώσασθαι, the aorist middle of ἀπωθέω ‘push away from oneself’, with παρὰ νηῶν ‘from beside the ships’. παυροτέρους περ ἐόντας ‘even though they were fewer’ is accusative plural, agreeing with the Trojans: though outnumbered, the Trojans cannot be pushed off, and the Achaeans in turn do not give way.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ ποτε Τρῶες Δαναῶν ἐδύναντο φάλαγγας
ῥηξάμενοι κλισίῃσι μιγήμεναι ἠδὲ νέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
oude pote Trōes Danaōn edynanto phalangas
rhēxamenoi klisiēisi migēmenai ēde neessin.
sentences.l:
nor ever could the Trojans the Danaans’ battle-lines
having broken, mix with the huts and ships.
sentences.i: and the Trojans, for their part, could never break the Danaans’ battle-lines and get in among the huts and ships.
sentences.n: οὐδέ ποτε … ἐδύναντο is ‘nor ever could’. ῥηξάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, and Δαναῶν φάλαγγας is ‘the Danaans’ battle-lines’. μιγήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of μίγνυμι ‘mingle’, with the datives κλισίῃσι ‘huts’ and νέεσσιν (the epic dative plural of νηῦς ‘ship’), so ‘to get in among the huts and ships’; ἠδέ is ‘and’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὥς τε στάθμη δόρυ νήϊον ἐξιθύνει
τέκτονος ἐν παλάμῃσι δαήμονος, ὅς ῥά τε πάσης
εὖ εἰδῇ σοφίης ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν Ἀθήνης,
sentences.tr:
all’ hōs te stathmē dory nēïon exithynei
tektonos en palamēisi daēmonos, hos rha te pasēs
eu eidēi sophiēs hypothēmosynēisin Athēnēs,
sentences.l:
But as a line a ship’s timber makes straight
in the hands of a skilled builder, who all
craft well knows by the instructions of Athena,
sentences.i: But as the line makes a ship’s timber true in the hands of a skilled builder, who knows every craft well from the instructions of Athena,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὥς τε ‘but as when’ opens a simile that ends in the next line. στάθμη is a builder’s line (a cord used to mark a straight edge); δόρυ νήϊον is ‘a ship’s timber’ (νήϊος ‘of a ship’), and ἐξιθύνει is ‘makes straight’, a general present. τέκτονος … δαήμονος is ‘of a skilled builder’ (δαήμων ‘knowing’; τέκτων covers working in wood as well as building, and a ship’s timber is a wright’s work), ἐν παλάμῃσι ‘in the hands’. ὅς ῥά τε … εὖ εἰδῇ is a general relative clause with a subjunctive, ‘who knows well’; σοφίης πάσης ‘all craft’ is the genitive after it, and ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν Ἀθήνης is ‘by the instructions of Athena’, the goddess of crafts.

sentences.t: ὣς μὲν τῶν ἐπὶ ἶσα μάχη τέτατο πτόλεμός τε·
sentences.tr: hōs men tōn epi isa machē tetato ptolemos te·
sentences.l: so of them equally the fighting was stretched, and the war;
sentences.i: so the fighting and the war were stretched out evenly between them;
sentences.n: ὣς … ‘so’ finishes the simile: as the line keeps the timber true, the fighting is held level. τῶν is ‘of them’, the two armies; ἐπὶ ἶσα is ‘evenly, on equal terms’; μάχη τέτατο is ‘the fighting was stretched’, the pluperfect passive of τείνω; and πτόλεμος is the epic form of πόλεμος ‘war’. The same line stands in an earlier part, which goes on differently.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοι δ’ ἀμφ’ ἄλλῃσι μάχην ἐμάχοντο νέεσσιν,
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἄντ’ Αἴαντος ἐείσατο κυδαλίμοιο.
sentences.tr:
alloi d’ amph’ allēisi machēn emachonto neessin,
Hektōr d’ ant’ Aiantos eeisato kydalimoio.
sentences.l:
and others about other ships fought a fight,
but Hector against Ajax rushed, the glorious.
sentences.i: Others fought their fight around other ships, but Hector rushed straight at glorious Ajax.
sentences.n: ἄλλοι … ἄλλῃσι … νέεσσιν is ‘others around other ships’, and μάχην ἐμάχοντο is a cognate accusative, ‘fought a fight’. Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἄντ’ Αἴαντος ἐείσατο is ‘Hector rushed at Ajax’: ἐείσατο is the aorist middle of ἵεμαι ‘speed’, and ἄντα (elided) with the genitive is ‘face to face with’. κυδαλίμοιο ‘glorious’ is genitive, agreeing with Αἴαντος; κυδάλιμος and φαίδιμος (in 419) are both ‘glorious’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ μιῆς περὶ νηὸς ἔχον πόνον, οὐδὲ δύναντο
οὔθ’ ὃ τὸν ἐξελάσαι καὶ ἐνιπρῆσαι πυρὶ νῆα
οὔθ’ ὃ τὸν ἂψ ὤσασθαι, ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπέλασσέ γε δαίμων.
sentences.tr:
tō de miēs peri nēos echon ponon, oude dynanto
outh’ ho ton exelasai kai eniprēsai pyri nēa
outh’ ho ton aps ōsasthai, epei rh’ epelasse ge daimōn.
sentences.l:
and the two about one ship had the toil, nor were able,
not he to drive the other off and set the ship on fire with fire,
nor he to push the other back, since a power had brought near.
sentences.i: The two of them toiled over one ship, and neither could drive the other off and set the ship on fire, nor push the other back, since some power had brought them together.
sentences.n: τώ δέ ‘and the two’ (dual) are Hector and Ajax, who struggle over one ship (μιῆς … νηός, the genitive of μία, with περί ‘about’). ἔχον πόνον is ‘had the toil’, and δύναντο is the unaugmented imperfect of δύναμαι. οὔθ’ ὃ τὸν … οὔθ’ ὃ τὸν is ‘neither the one … the other, nor the one … the other’, with ὁ and τόν as demonstratives: Hector cannot drive Ajax away (ἐξελάσαι) and burn the ship (ἐνιπρῆσαι πυρί), nor can Ajax push Hector back (ὤσασθαι, aorist middle of ὠθέω ‘push’; ἂψ ‘back’). ἐπεὶ ῥ’ ἐπέλασσέ γε δαίμων is ‘since some power had brought near’: the object of ἐπέλασσε (aorist of ἐπελάζω) is left unsaid, most naturally the two men, and δαίμων is an unnamed god acting on them.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ υἷα Κλυτίοιο Καλήτορα φαίδιμος Αἴας
πῦρ ἐς νῆα φέροντα κατὰ στῆθος βάλε δουρί.
sentences.tr:
enth’ huia Klytioio Kalētora phaidimos Aias
pyr es nēa pheronta kata stēthos bale douri.
sentences.l:
Then the son of Clytius, Caletor, glorious Ajax
bringing fire to the ship, in the chest struck with a spear.
sentences.i: Then glorious Ajax struck Caletor, son of Clytius, in the chest with his spear as he was bringing fire to the ship.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘then’. υἷα is the epic accusative of υἱός ‘son’, Κλυτίοιο the epic genitive in -οιο, and Καλήτορα is in apposition, the object of βάλε. φέροντα agrees with Καλήτορα: ‘bringing fire to the ship’ (πῦρ ἐς νῆα). κατὰ στῆθος is ‘in the chest’, βάλε the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω ‘strike’, and δουρί the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, δαλὸς δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρός.
sentences.tr: doupēsen de pesōn, dalos de hoi ekpese cheiros.
sentences.l: And he fell with a thud, and the brand fell out of his hand.
sentences.i: He fell with a thud, and the brand dropped from his hand.
sentences.n: δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω ‘fall with a thud’, the heavy sound of a man collapsing in armour, and πεσών is ‘falling’. δαλός is a ‘brand’, here the burning torch he was carrying, and οἱ ‘from him’ goes with ἔκπεσε χειρός ‘fell from his hand’ (genitive of separation).

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὡς ἐνόησεν ἀνεψιὸν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
ἐν κονίῃσι πεσόντα νεὸς προπάροιθε μελαίνης,
Τρωσί τε καὶ Λυκίοισιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ hōs enoēsen anepsion ophthalmoisin
en koniēisi pesonta neos proparoithe melainēs,
Trōsi te kai Lykioisin ekekleto makron aÿsas·
sentences.l:
And Hector, when he noticed his cousin with his eyes
in the dust fallen before a black ship,
to the Trojans and Lycians called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And when Hector saw with his eyes his cousin fallen in the dust before a black ship, he gave orders to the Trojans and Lycians, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: ἐνόησεν … ἀνεψιόν is ‘noticed his cousin’: Caletor is Hector’s cousin. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is ‘with his eyes’, ἐν κονίῃσι ‘in the dust’ (plural in the Greek), and νεὸς προπάροιθε μελαίνης ‘in front of a black ship’. ἐκέκλετο is a reduplicated aorist middle of κέλομαι ‘call, urge’, and μακρὸν ἀΰσας is ‘shouting loudly’ (the aorist participle of ἀΰω, with μακρόν as an adverb). Line 424 stands elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Δάρδανοι ἀγχιμαχηταὶ
μὴ δή πω χάζεσθε μάχης ἐν στείνεϊ τῷδε,
ἀλλ’ υἷα Κλυτίοιο σαώσατε, μή μιν Ἀχαιοὶ
τεύχεα συλήσωσι νεῶν ἐν ἀγῶνι πεσόντα.
sentences.tr:
Trōes kai Lykioi kai Dardanoi anchimachētai
mē dē pō chazesthe machēs en steineï tōide,
all’ huia Klytioio saōsate, mē min Achaioi
teuchea sylēsōsi neōn en agōni pesonta.
sentences.l:
“Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, close-fighters,
do not yet give way from the fight in this narrow place,
but the son of Clytius save, lest the Achaeans
strip his armour, fallen in the gathering of the ships.”
sentences.i: “Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, fighters at close quarters, do not yet give way from the fight in this narrow place, but save the son of Clytius, lest the Achaeans strip his armour as he lies fallen in the gathering-place of the ships.”
sentences.n: Hector’s speech. Δάρδανοι are the Dardanians, a Trojan people, and ἀγχιμαχηταί ‘close-fighters’ is the stock epithet. μὴ δή πω χάζεσθε is ‘do not yet give way’ (present imperative of χάζομαι, with μάχης as a genitive of separation, ‘from the fight’), ἐν στείνεϊ τῷδε ‘in this narrow place’ (στεῖνος, the crush by the ships). ἀλλ’ … σαώσατε is ‘but save’ (aorist imperative of σαόω), with υἷα Κλυτίοιο as its object. μή μιν … συλήσωσι is ‘lest they strip him’: μή with the subjunctive after an imperative states the fear, τεύχεα is the armour and πεσόντα ‘fallen’ agrees with μιν. νεῶν ἐν ἀγῶνι is ‘in the gathering-place of the ships’ (ἀγών ‘gathering’, the crowded ground by the ships). The first line stands in an earlier part.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν Αἴαντος ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn Aiantos akontise douri phaeinōi.
sentences.l: So having spoken, at Ajax he cast with his shining spear.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and cast his shining spear at Ajax.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, and the subject, Hector, is not named. Αἴαντος ἀκόντισε is ‘cast at Ajax’: ἀκοντίζω takes the genitive of its target. δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with the shining spear’ (δουρί, the epic dative of δόρυ).

sentences.t:
τοῦ μὲν ἅμαρθ’, ὃ δ’ ἔπειτα Λυκόφρονα Μάστορος υἱὸν
Αἴαντος θεράποντα Κυθήριον, ὅς ῥα παρ’ αὐτῷ
ναῖ’, ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα κατέκτα Κυθήροισι ζαθέοισι,
sentences.tr:
tou men hamarth’, ho d’ epeita Lykophrona Mastoros huion
Aiantos theraponta Kythērion, hos rha par’ autōi
nai’, epei andra katekta Kythēroisi zatheoisi,
sentences.l:
Him he missed, but he then Lycophron, Mastor’s son,
Ajax’s attendant, the Cytherian, who beside him
dwelt, since a man he had killed in most holy Cythera,
sentences.i: Hector missed him, but Lycophron, son of Mastor, a man of Cythera and Ajax’s attendant, who lived beside him since he had killed a man in most holy Cythera,
sentences.n: τοῦ μὲν ἅμαρθ’ is ‘him he missed’: ἅμαρθ’ is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω with the genitive τοῦ (Ajax), and ὃ δ’ is Hector. The sentence goes on to the man he hit instead, Λυκόφρονα Μάστορος υἱόν ‘Lycophron, Mastor’s son’, whose verb comes in the next unit. θεράποντα is ‘attendant’, Κυθήριον ‘of Cythera’ (the island), and ὅς ῥα παρ’ αὐτῷ ναῖ’ is ‘who dwelt beside him’ (ναῖ’ is the elided imperfect of ναίω). ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα κατέκτα is ‘since he had killed a man’, in Κυθήροισι ζαθέοισι ‘most holy Cythera’ (the plural name Κύθηρα; ζαθέος ‘very holy’). The Greek gives the killing as the reason he lives with Ajax.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ἔβαλεν κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ οὔατος ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ
ἑσταότ’ ἄγχ’ Αἴαντος·
sentences.tr:
ton rh’ ebalen kephalēn hyper ouatos oxeï chalkōi
hestaot’ anch’ Aiantos·
sentences.l:
him he struck on the head above the ear with sharp bronze,
standing near Ajax;
sentences.i: Hector struck him on the head above the ear with sharp bronze as he stood near Ajax;
sentences.n: τόν ῥ’ ἔβαλεν ‘him he struck’: τόν takes up Lycophron, the long object of the previous unit. κεφαλὴν ὑπὲρ οὔατος is ‘on the head above the ear’ (κεφαλήν is the accusative of the part struck, οὔατος the genitive of οὖς), ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with sharp bronze’, and ἑσταότ’ the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, ἄγχ’ Αἴαντος ‘near Ajax’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος ἐν κονίῃσι
νηὸς ἄπο πρυμνῆς χαμάδις πέσε, λύντο δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hyptios en koniēisi
nēos apo prymnēs chamadis pese, lynto de guia.
sentences.l:
and he on his back in the dust
from the ship’s stern to the ground fell, and his limbs were loosened.
sentences.i: and he fell on his back in the dust, from the ship’s stern to the ground, and his limbs gave way.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Lycophron. ὕπτιος is ‘on his back’, ἐν κονίῃσι ‘in the dust’, νηὸς ἄπο πρυμνῆς ‘from the ship’s stern’ (ἄπο is ἀπό placed after its noun), and χαμάδις ‘to the ground’; πέσε is the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω. λύντο δὲ γυῖα ‘and his limbs were loosened’ is the formula of death: λύντο is the aorist middle of λύω, γυῖα ‘limbs’.

sentences.t: Αἴας δ’ ἐρρίγησε, κασίγνητον δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: Aias d’ errigēse, kasignēton de prosēuda·
sentences.l: And Ajax shuddered, and his brother he addressed:
sentences.i: Ajax shuddered, and spoke to his brother:
sentences.n: ἐρρίγησε is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’; the Greek does not say whether from horror or fear. κασίγνητον is ‘brother’, the accusative object of προσηύδα, the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. The brother, Teucer, is named in the first word of the speech.

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρε πέπον δὴ νῶϊν ἀπέκτατο πιστὸς ἑταῖρος
Μαστορίδης, ὃν νῶϊ Κυθηρόθεν ἔνδον ἐόντα
ἶσα φίλοισι τοκεῦσιν ἐτίομεν ἐν μεγάροισι·
sentences.tr:
Teukre pepon dē nōïn apektato pistos hetairos
Mastoridēs, hon nōï Kythērothen endon eonta
isa philoisi tokeusin etiomen en megaroisi·
sentences.i: “My good fellow Teucer, now our trusty companion, the son of Mastor, has been killed—he whom we two honoured in our halls, when he was with us from Cythera, as much as our own dear parents;
sentences.n: Ajax’s speech. Τεῦκρε πέπον is ‘Teucer, my good fellow’ (πέπον is a familiar form of address whose sense is not known). δὴ νῶϊν ἀπέκτατο is ‘now has been killed for us two’: νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘for us two’, and ἀπέκτατο the aorist of ἀποκτείνω with passive sense. πιστὸς ἑταῖρος Μαστορίδης is ‘trusty companion, Mastor’s son’ (the patronymic in -ίδης). ὃν νῶϊ … ἐτίομεν is ‘whom we two honoured’ (νῶϊ is the dual nominative), Κυθηρόθεν ‘from Cythera’ (the ending -θεν means ‘from’), ἔνδον ἐόντα ‘when he was within’, ἶσα φίλοισι τοκεῦσιν ‘equally with dear parents’, ἐν μεγάροισι ‘in the halls’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἕκτωρ μεγάθυμος ἀπέκτανε.
sentences.tr: ton d’ Hektōr megathymos apektane.
sentences.l: and him Hector, great-hearted, has killed.
sentences.i: Great-hearted Hector has killed him.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ‘and him’ points back to Lycophron; the subject comes after it, Ἕκτωρ μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted Hector’, with the stock epithet. ἀπέκτανε is the aorist of ἀποκτείνω. The sentence ends in the middle of the line, and a new question begins in the same line.

sentences.t:
ποῦ νύ τοι ἰοὶ
ὠκύμοροι καὶ τόξον ὅ τοι πόρε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων;
sentences.tr:
pou ny toi ioi
ōkymoroi kai toxon ho toi pore Phoibos Apollōn;
sentences.l:
Where now are your arrows, swift-doomed,
and the bow which gave you Phoebus Apollo?”
sentences.i: Where now are your arrows that bring swift doom, and the bow that Phoebus Apollo gave you?”
sentences.n: ποῦ νύ τοι ἰοί is ‘where now are your arrows’ (τοι is σοι, ἰοί the plural of ἰός ‘arrow’). ὠκύμοροι is from ὠκύς ‘swift’ and μόρος ‘doom’; of arrows it must mean bringing swift doom to the man hit (of Achilles it means swift to his own doom). τόξον ὅ τοι πόρε is ‘the bow that gave you’: ὅ is the relative, and πόρε the unaugmented aorist of πορεῖν ‘give’. Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the archer god, so the question is also a reproach.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὃ δὲ ξυνέηκε, θέων δέ οἱ ἄγχι παρέστη,
τόξον ἔχων ἐν χειρὶ παλίντονον ἠδὲ φαρέτρην
ἰοδόκον·
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho de xyneēke, theōn de hoi anchi parestē,
toxon echōn en cheiri palintonon ēde pharetrēn
iodokon·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Teucer understood, and ran and stood close beside him, holding in his hand the back-stretched bow and the arrow-holding quiver;
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (φάθ’ is the elided, unaugmented φάτο), and ὃ δὲ ξυνέηκε ‘and he understood’ has Teucer for its subject (ξυνέηκε is the aorist of συνίημι ‘understand’, and the understanding leads at once to action). θέων is ‘running’, and οἱ ἄγχι παρέστη ‘stood close beside him’. τόξον … παλίντονον is ‘the back-stretched bow’, and φαρέτρην ἰοδόκον is ‘the quiver, arrow-receiving’ (ἰός ‘arrow’ with the root of δέχομαι ‘receive’).

sentences.t: μάλα δ’ ὦκα βέλεα Τρώεσσιν ἐφίει.
sentences.tr: mala d’ ōka belea Trōessin ephiei.
sentences.l: and very quickly shafts at the Trojans he kept sending.
sentences.i: and very quickly he kept shooting shafts at the Trojans.
sentences.n: μάλα δ’ ὦκα is ‘and very quickly’. βέλεα is the uncontracted plural of βέλος ‘shaft’, Τρώεσσιν the dative plural, and ἐφίει the imperfect of ἐφίημι ‘let fly at’, so Teucer shoots again and again. The next lines give one of his hits.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ἔβαλε Κλεῖτον Πεισήνορος ἀγλαὸν υἱὸν
Πουλυδάμαντος ἑταῖρον ἀγαυοῦ Πανθοΐδαο
ἡνία χερσὶν ἔχοντα·
sentences.tr:
kai rh’ ebale Kleiton Peisēnoros aglaon huion
Poulydamantos hetairon agauou Panthoïdao
hēnia chersin echonta·
sentences.i: And he struck Cleitus, the splendid son of Peisenor, companion of noble Polydamas, son of Panthous, as he held the reins in his hands;
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ ἔβαλε ‘and he struck’, with Teucer as subject. Κλεῖτον Πεισήνορος ἀγλαὸν υἱόν is ‘Cleitus, Peisenor’s splendid son’ (ἀγλαός ‘splendid’). ἑταῖρον ‘companion’ is in apposition, and ἀγαυοῦ ‘noble’ goes with Πουλυδάμαντος, the genitive of Πουλυδάμας, whose nominative stands in 454; Πανθοΐδαο is the patronymic in -αο, ‘son of Panthous’. ἡνία χερσὶν ἔχοντα is ‘holding the reins in his hands’.

sentences.t: ὃ μὲν πεπόνητο καθ’ ἵππους·
sentences.tr: ho men peponēto kath’ hippous·
sentences.l: he had been busied with the horses;
sentences.i: he had been busy with the horses;
sentences.n: πεπόνητο is the pluperfect passive of πονέω ‘labour, be busy’, and καθ’ ἵππους is ‘about the horses’ (κατά with the accusative), so Cleitus was driving. ὃ μὲν has no δέ answering it directly; the story goes on in the next lines with τάχα δ’.

sentences.t:
τῇ γὰρ ἔχ’ ᾗ ῥα πολὺ πλεῖσται κλονέοντο φάλαγγες
Ἕκτορι καὶ Τρώεσσι χαριζόμενος·
sentences.tr:
tēi gar ech’ hēi rha poly pleistai kloneonto phalanges
Hektori kai Trōessi charizomenos·
sentences.l:
for he was holding where by far the most battle-lines were being thrown into confusion,
gratifying Hector and the Trojans;
sentences.i: for he was driving where by far the most battle-lines were being thrown into confusion, to gratify Hector and the Trojans;
sentences.n: τῇ … ᾗ is ‘there … where’. ἔχ’ is the elided ἔχε ‘he held’, with his course understood, so ‘he was driving there’. πολὺ πλεῖσται κλονέοντο φάλαγγες is ‘by far the most battle-lines were in turmoil’ (κλονέω ‘throw into confusion’, here passive, ‘were being thrown into confusion’; φάλαγγες ‘battle-lines’). Ἕκτορι καὶ Τρώεσσι χαριζόμενος is ‘gratifying Hector and the Trojans’ (χαρίζομαι with the dative, ‘do a favour to’): Cleitus drove into the thick of the fight to please them.

sentences.t:
τάχα δ’ αὐτῷ
ἦλθε κακόν, τό οἱ οὔ τις ἐρύκακεν ἱεμένων περ.
sentences.tr:
tacha d’ autōi
ēlthe kakon, to hoi ou tis erykaken hiemenōn per.
sentences.l:
and soon to him came evil, which for him
not anyone held back, though eager.
sentences.i: and soon evil came upon him, which none could hold back from him, however eager they were.
sentences.n: τάχα δ’ αὐτῷ ἦλθε κακόν is ‘and soon evil came to him’, and τό is the relative ‘which’. οὔ τις ἐρύκακεν is ‘none held back’ (ἐρύκακε is a reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω), and ἱεμένων περ ‘though they were eager’ is a genitive plural, ‘of those who wished it’, his companions. The ‘evil’ is the arrow of the next line.

sentences.t: αὐχένι γάρ οἱ ὄπισθε πολύστονος ἔμπεσεν ἰός·
sentences.tr: aucheni gar hoi opisthe polystonos empesen ios·
sentences.l: for in his neck from behind the much-groaning arrow fell;
sentences.i: for in his neck from behind the arrow of the many groans struck home;
sentences.n: αὐχένι … οἱ ὄπισθε is ‘in his neck, from behind’ (αὐχένι the dative of αὐχήν ‘neck’, οἱ ‘his’). ἔμπεσεν is the aorist of ἐμπίπτω ‘fall into’, so the arrow lodged there. πολύστονος is πολύς ‘many’ with στόνος ‘groan’; of an arrow it means causing many groans.

sentences.t:
ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, ὑπερώησαν δέ οἱ ἵπποι
κείν’ ὄχεα κροτέοντες.
sentences.tr:
ēripe d’ ex ocheōn, hyperōēsan de hoi hippoi
kein’ ochea kroteontes.
sentences.l:
And he fell out of the chariot, and swerved aside from him the horses,
rattling the empty chariot.
sentences.i: He fell from the chariot, and the horses shied away from him, rattling the empty chariot.
sentences.n: ἤριπε is the aorist of ἐρείπω ‘fall, crash down’, and ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘out of the chariot’ (the plural ὄχεα stands for one chariot). ὑπερώησαν is the aorist of ὑπερωέω ‘swerve aside’, said of the horses. κείν’ ὄχεα κροτέοντες is ‘rattling the empty chariot’ (κείν’ is κενά ‘empty’, κροτέω ‘make rattle’). The first half of the line stands in an earlier part.

sentences.t:
ἄναξ δ’ ἐνόησε τάχιστα
Πουλυδάμας, καὶ πρῶτος ἐναντίος ἤλυθεν ἵππων.
sentences.tr:
anax d’ enoēse tachista
Poulydamas, kai prōtos enantios ēlythen hippōn.
sentences.l:
And the lord noticed it most quickly,
Polydamas, and first came face to face with the horses.
sentences.i: Lord Polydamas noticed it very quickly, and was the first to come face to face with the horses.
sentences.n: ἄναξ … Πουλυδάμας is ‘lord Polydamas’, the name held back to the start of the next line. ἐνόησε τάχιστα is ‘noticed very quickly’ (the superlative adverb). καὶ πρῶτος ἐναντίος ἤλυθεν ἵππων is ‘and first came face to face with the horses’ (ἐναντίος with the genitive; ἤλυθεν is the epic form of ἦλθεν).

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ὅ γ’ Ἀστυνόῳ Προτιάονος υἱέϊ δῶκε,
πολλὰ δ’ ἐπότρυνε σχεδὸν ἴσχειν εἰσορόωντα
ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
tous men ho g’ Astynoōi Protiaonos huieï dōke,
polla d’ epotryne schedon ischein eisoroōnta
hippous·
sentences.i: He gave them to Astynous, the son of Protiaon, and urged him strongly to keep the horses close at hand and watch them;
sentences.n: τοὺς μὲν is ‘these’, the horses named at the end in ἵππους; ὅ γ’ is Polydamas. Ἀστυνόῳ Προτιάονος υἱέϊ is ‘to Astynous, Protiaon’s son’, and δῶκε is ‘gave’. πολλὰ ἐπότρυνε is ‘urged strongly’ (πολλά used as an adverb). σχεδὸν ἴσχειν εἰσορόωντα is ‘to keep close, watching’: ἴσχειν ‘hold’, and εἰσορόωντα is accusative singular, agreeing with the man urged.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς δ’ αὖτις ἰὼν προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη.
sentences.tr: autos d’ autis iōn promachoisin emichthē.
sentences.l: and himself, going back again, among the front-fighters mingled.
sentences.i: and he himself went back and mingled with the foremost fighters.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς δ’ ‘but he himself’ is Polydamas. αὖτις ἰών is ‘going back again’, and προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη ‘mingled with the front-fighters’ (the aorist passive of μίγνυμι with the dative): he returns to the front rank.

sentences.t:
Τεῦκρος δ’ ἄλλον ὀϊστὸν ἐφ’ Ἕκτορι χαλκοκορυστῇ
αἴνυτο, καί κεν ἔπαυσε μάχης ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν,
εἴ μιν ἀριστεύοντα βαλὼν ἐξείλετο θυμόν.
sentences.tr:
Teukros d’ allon oïston eph’ Hektori chalkokorystēi
ainyto, kai ken epause machēs epi nēusin Achaiōn,
ei min aristeuonta balōn exeileto thymon.
sentences.l:
And Teucer another arrow at Hector, bronze-armed,
was taking, and would have made him cease from fighting at the ships of the Achaeans,
if, as he excelled, striking him he had taken out his life.
sentences.i: Teucer took up another arrow against Hector, armed in bronze, and would have stopped his fighting at the ships of the Achaeans, if he had struck him while he was excelling and taken his life.
sentences.n: Τεῦκρος δ’ begins a new action. ἄλλον ὀϊστόν is ‘another arrow’ (the edition prints the diaeresis), ἐφ’ Ἕκτορι χαλκοκορυστῇ ‘against Hector, armed in bronze’, and αἴνυτο is the imperfect middle of αἴνυμαι ‘take up’. καί κεν ἔπαυσε … εἰ … ἐξείλετο is a past unreal condition: ‘and he would have stopped … if he had taken out’. μάχης is a genitive of separation, ‘from fighting’. μιν ἀριστεύοντα is ‘him as he excelled’, the verb meaning to be the best in fighting, and ἐξείλετο θυμόν is ‘took out his life’ (aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω; θυμός is ‘life’ when it leaves the body), with βαλών ‘having struck’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ λῆθε Διὸς πυκινὸν νόον, ὅς ῥ’ ἐφύλασσεν
Ἕκτορ’, ἀτὰρ Τεῦκρον Τελαμώνιον εὖχος ἀπηύρα,
sentences.tr:
all’ ou lēthe Dios pykinon noon, hos rh’ ephylassen
Hektor’, atar Teukron Telamōnion euchos apēura,
sentences.l:
but he did not escape the close-packed mind of Zeus, who was guarding
Hector, and from Telamonian Teucer took away the boast,
sentences.i: but he did not escape the shrewd mind of Zeus, who was guarding Hector, and robbed Telamonian Teucer of his triumph,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐ λῆθε is ‘but did not escape the notice of’ (λῆθε is the unaugmented aorist of λανθάνω, with the accusative of the person). Διὸς πυκινὸν νόον is ‘the close-packed mind of Zeus’, πυκινός being ‘close-packed’ and so ‘shrewd’ of a mind. ὅς ῥ’ ἐφύλασσεν Ἕκτορ’ is ‘who was guarding Hector’. Τελαμώνιον is the adjective ‘Telamonian’, ‘son of Telamon’, and ἀπαυράω ‘take away from’ takes two accusatives, so Τεῦκρον … εὖχος is ‘took the boast from Teucer’; εὖχος is the thing boasted of, the triumph. The subject of ἀπηύρα is Zeus.

sentences.t:
ὅς οἱ ἐϋστρεφέα νευρὴν ἐν ἀμύμονι τόξῳ
ῥῆξ’ ἐπὶ τῷ ἐρύοντι·
sentences.tr:
hos hoi eÿstrephea neurēn en amymoni toxōi
rhēx’ epi tōi eryonti·
sentences.l:
who for him the well-twisted string in the blameless bow
broke, as he was drawing it;
sentences.i: who broke the well-twisted string on his blameless bow as he was drawing it;
sentences.n: ὅς ‘who’ is still Zeus. ῥῆξ’ is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is Teucer. ἐϋστρεφέα νευρήν is ‘the well-twisted string’ (the edition prints the diaeresis), and ἐν ἀμύμονι τόξῳ ‘on the blameless bow’: ἀμύμων is a stock epithet of unknown sense. ἐπὶ τῷ ἐρύοντι is ‘upon him as he drew it’, with the article used as a demonstrative and ἐρύω ‘draw’.

sentences.t:
παρεπλάγχθη δέ οἱ ἄλλῃ
ἰὸς χαλκοβαρής, τόξον δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρός.
sentences.tr:
pareplanchthē de hoi allēi
ios chalkobarēs, toxon de hoi ekpese cheiros.
sentences.l:
and was turned aside for him elsewhere
the arrow, bronze-heavy, and the bow from his hand fell out.
sentences.i: and the bronze-heavy arrow went astray in another direction, and the bow dropped from his hand.
sentences.n: παρεπλάγχθη is the aorist passive of παραπλάζω ‘turn aside, go astray’, and ἄλλῃ is ‘elsewhere’. ἰὸς χαλκοβαρής is ‘the bronze-heavy arrow’ (χαλκός ‘bronze’ with βαρύς ‘heavy’, the weight of its head). τόξον δέ οἱ ἔκπεσε χειρός is ‘and the bow fell from his hand’ (the same verb and construction as for Caletor’s brand).

sentences.t: Τεῦκρος δ’ ἐρρίγησε, κασίγνητον δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: Teukros d’ errigēse, kasignēton de prosēuda·
sentences.l: And Teucer shuddered, and his brother he addressed:
sentences.i: Teucer shuddered, and spoke to his brother:
sentences.n: The line repeats the line for Ajax with Teucer’s name in place of his, so the two brothers answer each other. ἐρρίγησε is ‘shuddered’ (the aorist of ῥιγέω), and κασίγνητον is ‘brother’, here Ajax, who is not named.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ δὴ πάγχυ μάχης ἐπὶ μήδεα κείρει
δαίμων ἡμετέρης, ὅ τέ μοι βιὸν ἔκβαλε χειρός,
sentences.tr:
ō popoi ē dē panchy machēs epi mēdea keirei
daimōn hēmeterēs, ho te moi bion ekbale cheiros,
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly indeed wholly the counsels for our fight cuts
a power, who from my hand the bow threw out,
sentences.i: “Ah, truly some power is wholly cutting away our counsels for the fight, he who has thrown the bow out of my hand,
sentences.n: Teucer’s speech. ὢ πόποι is ‘Ah’, an exclamation of dismay, and ἦ δὴ πάγχυ is ‘truly, wholly’. δαίμων is an unnamed divine power acting on men, the subject of κείρει ‘cuts, shears’. μάχης ἐπὶ μήδεα … ἡμετέρης is ‘counsels for our fight’, with μήδεα ‘counsels’ and ἡμετέρης ‘our’ agreeing with μάχης; the word order is split over the line. ὅ τέ μοι picks up the δαίμων again as ‘he who, for me’; βιόν is ‘bow’ (the accent tells it from βίος ‘life’), and ἔκβαλε χειρός is ‘threw out of my hand’, with the genitive of separation.

sentences.t:
νευρὴν δ’ ἐξέρρηξε νεόστροφον, ἣν ἐνέδησα
πρώϊον, ὄφρ’ ἀνέχοιτο θαμὰ θρῴσκοντας ὀϊστούς.
sentences.tr:
neurēn d’ exerrēxe neostrophon, hēn enedēsa
prōïon, ophr’ anechoito thama thrōiskontas oïstous.
sentences.l:
and the string burst off, newly twisted, which I fastened
early, so that it might bear the arrows leaping thick and fast.”
sentences.i: and has burst the newly twisted string that I fastened on early, so that it might bear up under the arrows leaping off it thick and fast.”
sentences.n: νευρὴν δ’ ἐξέρρηξε is ‘and burst the string’ (the aorist of ἐκρήγνυμι), νεόστροφον ‘newly twisted’ (νέος ‘new’ with στρέφω ‘twist’, the same root as ἐϋστρεφέα at 463). ἣν ἐνέδησα is ‘which I bound on’ (the aorist of ἐνδέω), and πρώϊον ‘early’. ὄφρ’ ἀνέχοιτο … ὀϊστούς: ὄφρα with the optative gives purpose after a past action, ‘so that it might bear’; ἀνέχομαι with the accusative is ‘hold up under, withstand’, θαμά ‘thick and fast’, and θρῴσκοντας ‘leaping’ describes the arrows as they spring from the bow. The part ends with the speech.
